# Sirach Chapter 7 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Sirach 7

---

1 Do no evil, and no evil will overtake you.

2 Stay clear of wrong, and it will stay clear of you.

3 Do not sow in the furrows of injustice, lest you reap it sevenfold.

4 Do not seek from the Lord a place of prominence, nor from the king a seat of honor.

5 Do not justify yourself before the Lord, nor try to seem wise before the king.

6 Do not seek to become a judge unless you have the strength to deal with injustice; otherwise you may show partiality to a powerful person and compromise your integrity.

7 Do not sin against the assembly of your city, and do not disgrace yourself before the people.

8 Do not give yourself over to repeating a sin, for it is not without consequence even once.

9 Do not say, "He will notice the many gifts I bring, and when I offer to the Most High God he will accept it."

10 Do not be halfhearted in your prayer, and do not neglect giving alms.

11 Do not mock a person who is bitter in spirit, for there is one who humbles and exalts.

12 Do not devise harm against your brother, nor against any friend or close neighbor.

13 Refuse to tell any kind of lie, for the habit brings no good.

14 Do not talk too much in the assembly of the elders, and do not repeat yourself in your prayers.

15 Do not despise hard work, and do not look down on the farming that the Most High established.

16 Do not count yourself among the ranks of sinners — remember that wrath does not delay.

17 Humble yourself greatly, for the punishment of the ungodly is fire and worms.

18 Do not barter a friend for money, nor a true brother for the gold of Ophir.

19 Do not dismiss a wife who is sensible and good, for her worth is more than gold.

20 Do not ill-treat a servant who works faithfully, nor a hired laborer who gives himself fully.

21 Treat a wise servant as you would a close friend; do not withhold his freedom from him.

22 If you have livestock, attend to them; if they are productive, keep them.

23 If you have children, discipline them and train them from an early age.

24 If you have daughters, keep watch over their bodies, and do not show excessive leniency toward them.

25 Give a daughter in marriage and you complete a great task — but give her to a man of understanding.

26 If you have a wife, do not put her away; but do not trust yourself to one you have come to resent.

27 Honor your father with all your heart, and do not forget your mother's birth pangs.

28 Remember that through them you came into being; what could you give them that would repay what they gave you?

29 Fear the Lord with all your soul, and hold his priests in reverence.

30 With all your strength love your Maker, and do not neglect his ministers.

31 Fear the Lord and honor the priest; give him his portion as commanded: the firstfruits, the guilt offering, the shoulder portion, the sacrifice of consecration, and the firstfruits of the holy offerings.

32 Also extend your hand to the poor, so that your blessing may be complete.

33 Give graciously to all the living, and do not withhold kindness from the dead.

34 Do not hold back from those who weep, and mourn with those who mourn.

35 Do not hesitate to visit the sick, for by such acts you will be loved.

36 In all you do, remember your last end, and you will never sin.

---

## Council Notes

**On v.19 — "do not dismiss a wife who is sensible and good":** Ben Sira's most surprising domestic pronouncement. He is not a romantic; he values a wife for intelligence (Greek syneti) and good character. SOPHIA preserves both adjectives: "sensible and good."

**On v.31 — priestly offerings:** Ben Sira is priestly-conservative. He lists specific temple obligations. These are Second Temple categories: firstfruits (aparche), guilt offering (prosophora), shoulder portion of sacrificed animals, sacrifices of consecration, and holy firstfruits. SOPHIA follows EMET's liturgical precision.

**On v.36 — "remember your last end":** Greek mnēmoneue ta eschata sou. The capstone of the whole chapter. All the practical advice — on judges, wives, servants, children, priests, the poor, the sick — is gathered under a single perspective: mortality. This is classic wisdom theology.

**On v.33 — "kindness from the dead":** Ben Sira refers to proper burial and mourning customs — acts of hesed for the deceased. PNEUMA's "don't withdraw your kindness even from the dead" captures this well.
